title: Midmarket Conversation Cheatsheet - Q3 Iter 1
content:
Goal: short, actionable enablement reference for AE/SDR to run efficient discovery -> demo -> close conversations for mid-market prospects (50-500 FTEs) across product, platform, and infra buyers. Draft notes and slide outline for a 10-12 minute demo + 1-page battlecard summary.

Top-level positioning (one-liner for meeting open):
- "Redwood provides predictable, low-latency LLM inference at scale with a single API you can run hosted, on dedicated capacity, or privately in your network — so product teams avoid infrastructure debt while keeping cost and latency under control."

Who to target in mid-market deals:
- Product manager / AI PM (use cases, quality bar)
- Engineering manager or Head of ML infra (cost, throughput, latency)
- Platform/Cloud architect (security, VPC, compliance)
- Procurement/IT for contract terms at later stage

Core win themes (short bullets to repeat):
- Predictable economics: cost-per-request visibility, batching and cache levers, recommendations from Redwood Optimize.
- Production-ready runtime: GPU-optimized serving, KV cache, autoscaling, and SLA options on Dedicated.
- Unified API across environments: same dev experience for hosted -> dedicated -> private.
- Reliability fallback paths: model variants and region routing to keep app online.

10-12 minute demo flow (script bullets):
1) 60s intro: "Typical problem we see: models are fast in lab but balloon in cost or break in prod. Redwood standardizes serving so you get consistent latency and unit economics."
2) 90s architecture sketch: show hosted vs dedicated vs private lanes and routing policy example.
3) 3 minutes — Live demo: create a quick text-generation request on hosted API, toggle model variant to show latency/cost difference, enable prefix caching to show token reductions.
4) 2 minutes — Console: per-route cost and trace for a sample request; show rollout/canary toggle.
5) 90s — Failure/resilience example: simulate capacity fallback to a cheaper variant and show telemetry that alerts and auto-fallback.
6) 60s — Close: next steps (POC proposal, small dedicated pilot, security review).

One-page battlecard (talking points):
- Pain: unpredictable token spend, poor p99 latency, time-consuming infra ops for serving.
- Redwood answer: measurable SLOs + tooling to trade cost vs latency + managed private option for compliance.
- Top competitors and quick differentiator lines:
  - Major cloud AI endpoints: broad infra but inconsistent cost optimizations and less ML-serving specialization. Redwood: inference-first optimizations and smarter routing.
  - In-house self-hosted stacks: full control but high ops cost and slow to iterate. Redwood: keep control via Private + lower ops via platform.
  - LLM API incumbents (fast simple APIs): great for prototypes, fewer options for reserved capacity and private deployments. Redwood: smooth path from prototype to enterprise SLA.

Objection handling (short scripts):
- "We can self-host cheaper." -> "How much eng time do you currently spend on model rollouts, kernel tuning, and serving reliability? Teams that benchmark total cost (infra+eng time) typically see Redwood reduce TCO by removing ops overhead and improving token efficiency via caching and quantization advice."
- "We need VPC/on-prem for compliance." -> "We support Private deployments with a customer-managed control plane and KMS integrations; we can scope a security review and a small pilot to validate network policies."
- "Pricing feels opaque." -> "We provide token-level breakdowns in the Console and can set pre-commit capacity and per-route quotas so spend is predictable during pilots."

Commercial anchors and pilots:
- Quick pilot option: 30-day hosted pilot (free tier credits) with up to X tokens and a simple success metric (p99 latency < 200ms or 20% reduction in per-token cost depending on use case).
- Small dedicated pilot: 3-month reserved capacity with negotiated commit and SLAs; good for predictable throughput teams.
- Legal checklist: standard SaaS + DPA; for Private include SOC/ISO questions and KMS/HSM notes.

Technical discovery checklist (questions to ask during discovery):
- App patterns: inference type (chat, gen, embedding, reranking); expected request size and concurrency; typical prompt lengths.
- Traffic profile: requests per minute, peak bursts, latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99).
- Data governance: PII concerns, retention needs, encryption at rest/in transit, region restrictions.
- Existing tooling: current model hosting approach, orchestration, monitoring, and cost reporting.

Demo prep checklist (for AEs):
- Pre-create demo account and sample app with realistic prompt set for prospect vertical.
- Prepare two model variants (cost-optimized and latency-optimized).
- Pre-populate Console with a synthetic route + cost traces to show during demo.
- Have rollback/canary example saved to show controlled rollout.

Email templates (short sequences):
- Intro email (to PM): short line about a common problem + ask for 20 min; include link to one-pager.
- Follow-up after demo: recap pain, suggested pilot option, ask to schedule security/architecture review with their infra lead.

KPIs to track for mid-market motion:
- Time from first demo to pilot start (goal < 21 days).
- Pilot-to-paid conversion rate (goal 40%+ for qualified mid-market).
- Average committed monthly spend for Dedicated pilots.
- Engineering time saved (qualitative feedback) and reduction in per-token cost post-pilot.

Roleplay snippets (use in training):
- AE: "Tell me about the biggest friction you hit when moving models to prod."
- PM: "Our latency is fine in testing but unpredictable at scale."
- AE: "We help teams pin down latency SLOs and give clear levers to trade cost — would you want to see an example with your prompt set?"

Open questions / TODOs for this draft:
- Define exact pilot token limit and credit size (Finance input needed).
- Replace placeholder legal checklist items with approved language from legal.
- Add recent benchmark numbers from Applied ML (request latest perf table).

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep this sheet short and skimmable; AEs should be able to glance and run a call.
- Avoid heavy architecture diagrams in the first call; use 1 simple slide and demo instead.
- Follow up with a one-pager tailored to vertical (support vs search vs productivity).

Version history: Iter 1 - initial mid-market cheatsheet focused on demo/detection flow and pilot framing.
